raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Purpose Fixes #43643 This PR introduces an optional ZeroMQ (ZMQ) metrics logger (`ZmqStatLogger`) allowing external monitoring systems to subscribe to real-time engine telemetry over a `zmq.PUB` socket. The eventual goal is to provide a lightweight alternative to Prometheus (by calling `/metrics`). Key Changes: 1. `ZmqStatLogger` & `ZmqMetricsStats`: - `ZmqStatLogger` drains a queue and broadcasts `msgspec`-encoded telemetry payloads over a ZMQ PUB socket in a background thread. - Publishes running request count, waiting request count, KV cache usage percentage, cache configuration info, and engine ID. This is an incomplete set of fields to showcase the design; more fields will be added in the future. 2. Observability & CLI Configuration: - Added `enable_zmq_metrics: bool = False` and `zmq_metrics_port: int = 5556` flags to `ObservabilityConfig`. 3. Engine Shutdown & Lifecycle Management: - Added `shutdown()` to `StatLoggerBase`, `StatLoggerManager`, `LLMEngine`, and `AsyncLLM` to cleanly close ZMQ sockets and join background publisher threads during server shutdown. _Note:_ The current implementation does not support DP yet; it assumes there is only one engine `engine_id=0`. ## Test Plan A [local standalone script](https://gist.github.com/azamikram/f91f5c329f3e0c698daa2c60e553ebd8) to test out the subscriber side: ```bash python3 subscribe_zmq_metrics.py --hosts host1:5556 host2:5556 ``` ## Test Result We added the subscriber support to `llm-d-router`. The following results are on three H100 nodes (TP=2) serving `Qwen/Qwen3-32B` under a bursty load. The HTTP baseline refers to the existing pull-based mechanism where the router periodically (after 50ms) polls the state from `/metrics`. The ZMQ implementation refers to the proposed push-based design. For HTTP baseline, we tried both Python and the Rust frontend for vLLM. Latency CDFs Throughput and CPU usage The key takeaways are that compared to HTTP-Python, push-based ZMQ metric support can: 1. **Reduce Tail Latency:** TTFT P99 improved by 16.20% (from 54.92s to 46.02s) and End-to-End P99 latency improved by 15.18%. 2. **Increase System Throughput:** Overall cluster token throughput rose by 18.44%. 3. **Lower Router Overhead:** Streaming binary msgpack frames over persistent sockets reduced the router CPU consumption by 64.51% and lowered P90 scheduling decision latency by 11.58%. ---
Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist - [X] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [X] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [X] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model.

Hi @tahsintunan, thanks for the review. I addressed all the comments you raised and the PR is ready for review again.

We considered building directly on top of `ZmqEventPublisher` in the backend, but chose a frontend `StatLogger` approach to unblock router integration while keeping PR scope minimal. There are two key factors that are different here:

1. Since metrics require the latest-state snapshots, in `ZmqStatLogger._publisher_thread`, we intentionally drain the queue to publish `latest_msg`, dropping intermediate states. `ZmqEventPublisher` streams _all_ events sequentially, which causes metric lag under backpressure.
2. The router currently uses Prometheus for state updates, implementing this as a `StatLogger` keeps ZMQ metrics co-located and consistent with `PrometheusStatLogger`.

Longer term however, we can refactor `ZmqEventPublisher` (or extract a shared ZMQ base class) to support queue draining, single-frame payloads, and optional sequence headers.

To avoid blocking the router work, I propose merging this frontend implementation first. I will open a follow-up issue to track the backend ZMQ publisher refactor.

@vMaroon, thanks! Could you please explain what you mean by the realtime comparison? Perhaps the following figure helps to answer your question. It shows the inter-arrival delay between updates received at the router using HTTP metrics collection and the proposed ZMQ publisher. Note that even though in most cases ZMQ has lower inter-arrival delay, the tail is much longer compared to a constant polling of HTTP metrics (50 ms). This is because with ZMQ we are able to push the updates after each step from the vllm side rather than router polling at a specific interval. You can find more detail about it in [this report.](https://docs.google.com/document/d/10Juqz_a-LhrOdpezV--NesW1KRHHIIEGV0of8xR7OX0/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.oohhob2wv1ep) cc: @zetxqx, @liu-cong

This pull request is from a fork — automated review is disabled. A repository maintainer can comment `@claude review` to run a one-time review.

Have you considered publishing engine-side instead of frontend-side? The running/waiting counts and KV usage originate in the scheduler, and the KV-events ZMQ publisher already lives there. That would make this work under both the Python and Rust frontends with no separate Rust work, avoid one publisher per API server process, and make DP natural. Each engine publishes, the router aggregates (the subscriber script already takes multiple hosts).

There may be reasons to prefer the frontend, so genuinely asking.

This needs the same `client_count > 1` guard as the default loggers above. With `--api-server-count > 1` each API server process binds the same port, so all but the first crash with EADDRINUSE at startup (and each client only sees a slice of the scheduler stats anyway). Suggest skip-and-warn.

+REQUIRED_ZMQ_METRICS_STATS_FIELDS = {
+    "num_requests_running",

+    "cache_config_info",
+    "engine_id",

+def test_zmq_metrics_stats_encoding_decoding():
+    """Test ZmqMetricsStats encoding and decoding with custom values,
+
+    verifying that the message has all and only the required fields.
+    """
+    stats = ZmqMetricsStats(
+        num_requests_running=5,
+        num_requests_waiting=10,
+        kv_cache_usage_perc=0.75,
+        cache_config_info={"block_size": 16, "num_gpu_blocks": 100},
+        engine_id="engine-0",
+    )
+
+    # Verify dataclass fields match REQUIRED_ZMQ_METRICS_STATS_FIELDS
+    dataclass_field_names = {f.name for f in fields(ZmqMetricsStats)}
+    assert dataclass_field_names == REQUIRED_ZMQ_METRICS_STATS_FIELDS
+
+    # Encode message
+    encoder = msgspec.msgpack.Encoder()
+    payload = encoder.encode(stats)
+
+    # Decode payload into a dict and verify keys
+    decoded_dict = msgspec.msgpack.decode(payload)
+    assert isinstance(decoded_dict, dict)
+    assert set(decoded_dict.keys()) == REQUIRED_ZMQ_METRICS_STATS_FIELDS
+
+    # Verify content
+    assert decoded_dict["num_requests_running"] == 5
+    assert decoded_dict["num_requests_waiting"] == 10
+    assert decoded_dict["kv_cache_usage_perc"] == 0.75
+    assert decoded_dict["cache_config_info"] == {
+        "block_size": 16,
+        "num_gpu_blocks": 100,
+    }
+    assert decoded_dict["engine_id"] == "engine-0"
+
+    # Decode into ZmqMetricsStats dataclass
+    decoded_stats = msgspec.msgpack.decode(payload, type=ZmqMetricsStats)
+    assert decoded_stats == stats
+

+

+
+    assert decoded_dict["num_requests_running"] == 0

+    assert decoded_dict["engine_id"] is None
+

+        if vllm_config.cache_config is not None:

+        self.queue: queue.Queue[ZmqMetricsStats | None] = queue.Queue()

+        self._ctx = zmq.Context.instance()

+            self._pub.connect(endpoint)

+        self._thread = threading.Thread(
+            target=self._publisher_thread,
+            daemon=True,
+            name="zmq-metrics-publisher",
+        )
+        self._thread.start()
+
+    def record(
+        self,

+        iteration_stats: IterationStats | None,

+        msg = ZmqMetricsStats(

+            num_requests_waiting=scheduler_stats.num_waiting_reqs,
+            kv_cache_usage_perc=scheduler_stats.kv_cache_usage,
+            cache_config_info=self.cache_config_info,

+
+    def _publisher_thread(self) -> None:
+        encoder = msgspec.msgpack.Encoder()
+
+        while self.running:
+            try:
+                msg = self.queue.get()
+                if msg is None:
+                    break
+
+                # Drain the queue to get the latest message
+                latest_msg = msg
+                try:

+                        if next_item is None:

+

Hi @tahsintunan, thanks for the review. I addressed all the comments you raised and the PR is ready for review again.

We considered building directly on top of `ZmqEventPublisher` in the backend, but chose a frontend `StatLogger` approach to unblock router integration while keeping PR scope minimal. There are two key factors that are different here:

1. Since metrics require the latest-state snapshots, in `ZmqStatLogger._publisher_thread`, we intentionally drain the queue to publish `latest_msg`, dropping intermediate states. `ZmqEventPublisher` streams _all_ events sequentially, which causes metric lag under backpressure.
2. The router currently uses Prometheus for state updates, implementing this as a `StatLogger` keeps ZMQ metrics co-located and consistent with `PrometheusStatLogger`.

Longer term however, we can refactor `ZmqEventPublisher` (or extract a shared ZMQ base class) to support queue draining, single-frame payloads, and optional sequence headers.

To avoid blocking the router work, I propose merging this frontend implementation first. I will open a follow-up issue to track the backend ZMQ publisher refactor.
This can be very useful - @azamikram can you provide a comparison that shows realtime-ness of this path of consumption + scale?

@vMaroon, thanks! Could you please explain what you mean by the realtime comparison? Perhaps the following figure helps to answer your question. It shows the inter-arrival delay between updates received at the router using HTTP metrics collection and the proposed ZMQ publisher. Note that even though in most cases ZMQ has lower inter-arrival delay, the tail is much longer compared to a constant polling of HTTP metrics (50 ms). This is because with ZMQ we are able to push the updates after each step from the vllm side rather than router polling at a specific interval. You can find more detail about it in [this report.](https://docs.google.com/document/d/10Juqz_a-LhrOdpezV--NesW1KRHHIIEGV0of8xR7OX0/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.oohhob2wv1ep) cc: @zetxqx, @liu-cong

## Claude Code Review

This pull request is from a fork — automated review is disabled. A repository maintainer can comment `@claude review` to run a one-time review.

Have you considered publishing engine-side instead of frontend-side? The running/waiting counts and KV usage originate in the scheduler, and the KV-events ZMQ publisher already lives there. That would make this work under both the Python and Rust frontends with no separate Rust work, avoid one publisher per API server process, and make DP natural. Each engine publishes, the router aggregates (the subscriber script already takes multiple hosts).

There may be reasons to prefer the frontend, so genuinely asking.
